There is a particular hour in late autumn when the sky turns the color of old pewter and the windows of houses begin to glow from within. It’s not quite evening, not quite twilight, but a threshold. At that hour, walking along streets I have known all my life, I sometimes feel that every lamppost, every mossy curb, every doorway has been waiting for me to arrive in exactly this state of mind. I cannot prove this. Memory is not proof. But standing still in the middle of the sidewalk, with the first cold breath of night on my face, I am certain of something: that we live less in houses than in the stories we tell ourselves about them. The walls are real. The roof is real. But the home is a kind of remembering—a practice of returning to the same coordinates with feeling, until those coordinates become inseparable from what we feel. Sometimes I think we are built like cities. We keep districts of childhood, vacant lots of lost love, industrial stretches of work, theaters of improbable hope. Some neighborhoods are well maintained. Others are overgrown. Yet all of them are us.

This essay is not going to be about how to live, or about anything instructive. It is just a walk. It is an attempt to write freely, the way one might wander, letting one thing lead to another, trusting that a path will appear underfoot. In that spirit, let me start with a memory: I was about eleven years old, lying in the grass behind a house that has since been torn down, watching clouds make their slow, deliberate migrations across the August sky. There were bees. There was the smell of warm hay. There was a low sound—which I later learned was called “the roaring of the sun,” though perhaps it was only my own blood moving through my ears. At that moment, I felt a strange and sudden tenderness toward the future, as if the person I would become were already standing somewhere beyond the horizon, waiting to meet me. I did not know his name. I did not know his worries. But I knew he would carry this afternoon inside him, preserved like a pressed flower between pages. And now here I am, older, carrying it. The afternoon is not really a precise visual image; it has blurred into a feeling. But the feeling is intact. And I wonder if that is what memory is for: to hold not the facts of our lives but their weather, not the song but the resonance.

When I try to understand why certain things remain while others vanish, I think of my grandmother’s kitchen. There was a yellow tablecloth, a radio playing a station no one ever named, and a shelf of mismatched cups. She is gone. The kitchen is gone. The house is gone, replaced by condominiums. But I can still summon the exact sound of her slippers on the linoleum, and the way she said “sit” as if it were the most important word in any language. I cannot recall the face of the neighbor who used to visit, though I saw her hundreds of times. I cannot recall what grade I was in when I first read a particular book. So much detail has been erased. Yet the emotional contour remains, precise as a fingerprint. This is the strangeness of memory: it is not a file cabinet but a sculptor, cutting away everything except the gesture, the expression, the moment of quiet recognition. Loss is part of its material. Forgetting is not the opposite of remembering; it is the chisel.

I want to write about forgetting because we tend to treat it as a betrayal, a failure, a leak in the vessel of the self. We buy books on memory, play brain games, fear the slippage of names. But what if forgetting is also mercy? What if the ability to shed the superfluous is exactly what lets us remain present? Think of how much you would be crushed by the full, unabridged record of your acquaintances, all their small humiliations, every embarrassment you ever caused, every sleepless night spent replaying a careless sentence. We could not bear it. We are designed for selective depth. The memory that matters is one that can recede, that can become something other than a raw recording—memory as metaphor, as lesson, as ache. To forget a face is not necessarily to lose a person; it may simply mean that the person has been absorbed into your way of moving through the world, the way food becomes flesh, the way water becomes cloud. Nothing is truly wasted. Not even what we fail to retrieve.

Language, too, is built on such absorption. We speak as inheritors of thousands of years of forgetting. Words carry fossils of meaning. The word “thrill,” for example, once meant to penetrate or pierce, and we can still feel that shiver in it, the idea that excitement enters us like a sharp point. The phrase “being beside oneself” suggests a self split in two, one version standing outside looking in. These linguistic remnants are memories we don’t remember remembering. I love to discover them the way archaeologists love potsherds—small, cracked, but enough to infer a whole vessel. A friend once told me that in Portuguese there is a word, *saudade*, for a longing for something that may never have existed, a melancholy nostalgia for a past that isn’t even yours. I felt I had known that word forever; I just didn’t have a name for it. Names matter. They give shape to interior weather. But they also fail. There are experiences for which we have no vocabulary, and maybe that is the deepest reason we write poems, compose music, photograph light on water. We are trying to build a bridge between the unsayable and the spoken—to make a word for the space before a word.

If I were to make a map of the places that matter to me, it would not look like a normal map. It would have enormous continents of boredom, tiny islands of ecstasy, rivers of recurring dreams, mountains made of books I read at seventeen. There would be a vast desert of waiting—waiting for buses, waiting for test results, waiting for phone calls, waiting to grow up. There would be an ocean of nighttime car rides. There would be a capital city that does not exist anywhere except in a language I invented at nine, and a border crossing where I once decided, without deliberation, to change my life. That decision is mostly invisible in the official biographical record. But it was more significant than any degree or job title. It happened in a parking lot, perhaps, or in a stairwell. It took no longer than a single heartbeat. And yet all that followed branched from it. This is another truth about memory: the most consequential moments are often the quietest. They do not announce themselves. They happen inside a pause, in the gap between two ordinary seconds. Later, we may call them turning points, but at the time they feel like nothing at all—like walking through a door you have walked through a thousand times, only this time the room on the other side has changed.

I think of this when I try to remember the beginning of a meaningful friendship. There was no thunderbolt. There was just a casual remark, a laugh, a shared umbrella, a question about a book. Later, I attempted to reconstruct the exact sequence and found that the earliest frames were blurred, as if the camera had not yet focused. What remained was the atmosphere: a sense of being recognized, of not having to explain everything, of finding that another person’s silence was comfortable rather than awkward. Friendship is a kind of collective memory, a story we co-author. We remember fragments differently, and the gaps between our versions are fertile ground. One of us remembers the joke, the other remembers the look that preceded it. And in that discrepancy, the relationship keeps growing. Because we are not one narrator; we are a duet.

It is tempting to believe that if only we could remember everything, we would truly know ourselves. But self-knowledge is not a matter of total recall. It is closer to curation. We decide—often unconsciously—what belongs in the gallery of our identity. We choose, or perhaps we are chosen by, certain images: the first snowfall of a year, a dog barking at two in the morning, the way a stranger smiled at us on a train. These images are not random. They are meaning-making machines. We stitch them together into a narrative, and that narrative is the self. Every act of storytelling is an act of forgetting as well as remembering. To tell a good story, you must leave things out. You must compress time, exaggerate details, skip the boring parts. This is not dishonesty. It is the only way to convey significance. If you described every minute of a day, the day would disappear beneath the detail. The true shape would be lost. So memory is an aesthetic practice. It is art, whether we admit it or not.

Art itself is an extended meditation on what remains. Painters capture light that can never last; writers fix feelings that would otherwise evaporate; musicians score emotion so it can be played again and again. We are, all of us, amateur preservationists. We take photographs, keep ticket stubs, save voice messages, write postcards that never get sent. When I was young, I believed these objects were keys—that they could unlock a direct re-experiencing of the past. Now I think they are not keys but triggers, small stones that we drop into the pond of memory, watching ripples spread. The photograph is not the moment. It is a fragment that allows the moment to be remade differently each time. I can look at a picture of my childhood backyard and feel not only the simple joy of that summer but also the shadow of all the summers that have come since. The object stays fixed; my response changes. This is one reason we keep returning to art: it offers a stable point around which our wandering minds can turn.

Yet even the most stable point dissolves. All things pass. I have become more aware of this over the years—not morbidly, but with a kind of deepening reverence. When I walk along the shore and see footprints filling with water, I think of how quickly the tide erases us. But then I notice that the beach itself is a memory of erosion, every grain of sand a stone that has forgotten its mountain. The mountain did not need to be remembered to become the strand. It gave up its solidity and was scattered, and in that scattering it found a new form. Perhaps we should not cling so tightly to who we are. Perhaps the goal is not to remain a mountain but to accept becoming sand, becoming sea, becoming air. This may sound like a counsel of despair, but I find it liberating. If I am ultimately forgettable—if everyone is—then I am free to act without obsessing over legacy. I can love without demanding to be loved forever. I can say goodbye without expecting to be remembered. I can do good work and release it into the world, knowing it may be repurposed, misread, or forgotten, and that this is exactly what should happen. Life is not a vault; it is a river. To try to store everything is to dam the flow.

I find an unexpected model for this in my own brain whenever it makes a mistake. I forget a name. I misplace my glasses. I walk into a room and forget why. These little failures used to annoy me. Now they seem almost instructive. They remind me that I am not a database; I am an organism. My attention is limited, and that limitation is the price of focus. To remember one thing, we must forget another. This is a profound trade-off. The neuroscientists tell us that forgetting is often an active process, not a passive decay; the brain prunes connections the way a gardener prunes roses, encouraging growth in the branches that matter. I like that image. Memory is not a record of everything that happened but of everything that shaped us. The rest is compost, and compost feeds the future. Without it, there would be no soil for new thoughts. Perhaps the forgotten conversations, the unremembered faces, the vanished rooms—they all fertilize the mind. They become nutrients we cannot see but are nourished by. They are the anonymous donors of our creativity.

Creativity itself is partly a matter of juxtaposing disparate memories. The surrealist poet Lautréamont famously defined beauty as the chance encounter of a sewing machine and an umbrella on a dissecting table. We laugh, but that synthesis is how thought happens. New ideas arise when we bring together elements that have never met: an insight from a novel, a recipe from a grandmother, a phrase overheard in a café, a dream that felt like a premonition. If we remembered everything in perfect order, we would miss the incongruities, the near-misses, the similarities across scales. Forgetting scrambles the archive. It puts the kitchen recipe next to the love letter, the geometry theorem next to the scent of lilac. And from that scramble, new meanings emerge. Our richest thinking is often born from a memory that is slightly out of place, an anchor that has drifted to a different harbor. This is why we should not be afraid to wander in our minds, to let the thread break, to follow a digression. Digression is not a failing of attention; it is the very engine of association. These pages, if they are anything, are an exercise in seeing where associations lead.

Let me follow one now. The word “threshold” comes from Old English, meaning a piece of wood across the bottom of a door. It also carries the sense of a boundary, the point where one enters a house, a room, a season. In many cultures thresholds are sacred; you carry the bride over them, you leave salt at them, you say farewell on them. My grandmother used to stand on her threshold and wave goodbye until our car turned the corner. She would stand there for what seemed a very long time, a small silhouette against the light of the hallway. That image is one of my clearest memories. It taught me something about constancy, about being seen off, about the fact that goodbyes can be a form of love performed from a fixed point. She is gone now; the threshold is gone. But when I close my eyes, she is still standing there, waving. It is a memory I have polished smooth with returning to it. It has become less a factual recollection and more a prayer. I can say thank you to that image, and it answers by keeping me company.

I could spend an entire essay listing such images: the red kite drifting over a field; the way a teacher wrote the date on a chalkboard; a certain quality of light in a hospital room; the wet smell of concrete after a storm; the sound of a bicycle chain being pedaled uphill; a list of groceries scribbled on the back of a receipt; a row of birds on a telephone wire. None of them are grand. Most are homely. Together, they form a private treasure, a mosaic whose full pattern only I can see. Yet if I were to write them down, they would become shareable. They would become public objects. Someone else might read them and recall their own red kite, their own chalkboard. In this way, the most specific memory becomes the most universal. We are all living in rooms lit by the same kind of light, holding the same kind of griefs, laughing at the same jokes, startled by the same impermanence. Our details differ, but the grammar is the same.

It is how we make a life from the rubble of experience. The tales we tell are not documentaries; they are lullabies, warnings, gifts. And every gift is incomplete, and every incompleteness is an invitation.

I would like to end, if I may, not with a conclusion but with another memory, a recent one. Last week, I walked to the top of a hill behind my apartment. There is no path; you just walk up through weeds and loose stones. At the top, there is a bench facing the town below. I sat there at sunset, watching the lights come on one by one. It was not a spectacular view. The town is not beautiful in any conventional way; it is a sprawl of rooftops and streetlights, a few church spires, a river reflecting a stripe of orange. But I recognized—with a startling clarity—that every one of those lights was a memory source. Behind each window, someone was cooking dinner, arguing, texting, reading, crying, praying, falling asleep. Their stories were invisible to me, but they were absolutely real. I could feel the weight of billions of small recollections accumulating under that sky: first steps, last breaths, apologies, proposals, endless repetitions of breakfast and dishes and doors. The universe, I thought, is made of such accumulations. Matter is memory in a different register. A tree is the memory of a seed; a rock is the memory of a volcano; I am the memory of a billion years of cells dividing and forgetting.

The wind was cold. I zipped my jacket and stood to go. As I started down the hill, I glanced over my shoulder at the bench, and for a second I imagined it was still occupied—not by me, but by all the versions of me that had ever climbed that hill, and all the people I had ever loved, and all the strangers whose lights I had ever counted. They were sitting there quietly, in a long row, like an audience, like a witness, like family. Then the light faded and they were gone. But the feeling lingered. I took it home with me. I am taking it with me now, into this essay, into your hands. Thank you for walking with me.

As I started down the hill, I glanced over my shoulder at the bench, and for a second I imagined it was still occupied—not by me, but by all the versions of me that had ever climbed that hill, and all the people I had ever loved, and all the strangers whose lights I had ever counted. They were sitting there quietly, in a long row, like an audience, like a witness, like family. Then the light faded and they were gone. But the feeling lingered. I took it home with me. I am taking it with me now, into this essay, into your hands. Thank you for walking with me.
